ap_statistics-m01.stem: A researcher plans to collect data from a random sample of adult members of a fitness center to answer the following investigative question: "What is the typical number of visits to the center in a month for adult members of a fitness center?" Which of the following best describes what this question asks about?

options.text: A question about the proportion of individuals in one category of a categorical variable
options.why: The question names one quantitative variable, not one categorical variable.

options.text: A question about the relationship between two quantitative variables
options.why: The question names one quantitative variable, not two quantitative variables.

options.text: A question about the distribution of one quantitative variable
options.why: The question names one quantitative variable, which is the structure this option describes.

options.text: A question about the association between two categorical variables
options.why: The question names one quantitative variable, not two categorical variables.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Recognize what an investigative question asks about: one distribution, a comparison of groups or an association
student_thinking: List the variables that the question names and decide whether each is quantitative or categorical
Match the number and types of variables, and whether groups are compared, to the one option with the same structure

key_conditions.condition: a valid investigative question names the variables it asks about, so its structure follows from the variables named
key_conditions.evidence: the question is stated in the stem and every option describes a different variable structure

misconceptions.description: names one variable when the question names two or the reverse
mixes up quantitative and categorical variables
mixes up comparing two groups with a relationship between two variables

verification.independent_path: the five question structures are generated from a table of (quantitative count, categorical count, groups compared) and exactly one row matches the question

ap_statistics-m02.stem: A student wants to study how long bus riders in a city wait at their stops. The student's first draft of an investigative question is: "Should the city add more buses to its routes?" Which of the following is the best revision that gives a valid investigative question requiring a statistical investigation?

options.text: Is waiting for a bus an unfair burden on the bus riders of the city?
options.why: Still asks for an opinion rather than for data that vary among individuals in a population.

options.text: How many bus routes does the city operate?
options.why: Asks for a single count that can be looked up, so no variability among individuals is anticipated.

options.text: How long did Ms. Alvarez wait at her bus stop this morning?
options.why: Asks about one individual, so there is no population and no variability to study.

options.text: What is the typical amount of time that bus riders in the city wait at their stops?
options.why: Keeps the topic of the draft, names the population, anticipates variability among the individuals and can be answered by collecting and analyzing data.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Diagnose why a draft question is not a valid investigative question and choose the revision that fixes it
student_thinking: Decide which property the draft lacks: variability among individuals, a population, or answerability with data
Choose the revision that has all three properties, not one that only rewords the flaw

key_conditions.condition: a valid investigative question anticipates variability, refers to a population and can be answered with data
key_conditions.evidence: the draft and each revision are stated in the stem and the options

misconceptions.description: keeps the flaw of the draft in new words
fixes the draft but introduces a different flaw
asks about one individual instead of a population

verification.independent_path: each revision is generated from the property table (variability, population, answerable with data); the draft flaw is one row, and exactly one revision has all three properties

ap_statistics-m03.stem: A researcher collects data on the number of days waiting for an appointment from a sample of $200$ patients selected at random from the records of all patients of one regional clinic. No treatment is assigned to anyone. Which of the following investigative questions can be answered using the data from this sample?

options.text: What is the typical number of days waiting for an appointment for patients of a clinic in another state?
options.why: The sample was not drawn from this population, so the data say nothing about it.

options.text: Would hiring more nurses cause patients to wait fewer days for an appointment?
options.why: A cause-and-effect question needs an experiment with random assignment, but the data come only from a random sample that was observed.

options.text: What is the typical number of days waiting for an appointment for all adults in the country?
options.why: The sample was drawn from a smaller population, so the data cannot be used to answer a question about this larger population.

options.text: What is the typical number of days waiting for an appointment for patients of the regional clinic?
options.why: The question refers to the population from which the sample was drawn at random, and it can be answered by summarizing the data collected.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Decide which investigative question the sample can answer from the population it was drawn from
student_thinking: Identify the population from which the sample was selected at random
Reject questions about a larger or different population and questions that need random assignment to answer

key_conditions.condition: data from a random sample can answer questions about the population sampled, and only an experiment supports cause and effect
key_conditions.evidence: the stem names the sampling frame and says that no treatment was assigned

misconceptions.description: applies the result to a larger population than the one sampled
applies the result to a population that was not sampled
asks a cause-and-effect question of observational data

verification.independent_path: the population of each question is compared with the sampling frame and the study type is checked against the claim; exactly one question matches both

ap_statistics-m04.stem: An interviewer in uniform asks a random sample of students whether they have ever cheated on an exam, with the principal standing nearby. Which of the following is the most likely source of bias in this study?

options.text: Nonresponse bias
options.why: Nonresponse bias occurs when individuals who were selected do not respond or cannot be reached. That is not what happens here: the setting may lead students to answer untruthfully.

options.text: Voluntary response bias
options.why: Voluntary response bias occurs when individuals choose for themselves whether to take part. That is not what happens here: the setting may lead students to answer untruthfully.

options.text: Undercoverage
options.why: Undercoverage occurs when some members of the population have no chance of being selected. That is not what happens here: the setting may lead students to answer untruthfully.

options.text: Response bias
options.why: Response bias occurs when individuals answer inaccurately, for example because of the wording of a question or the setting. In this scenario, the setting may lead students to answer untruthfully.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Identify the source of bias in a sampling plan from how individuals were selected and how they answered
student_thinking: Decide who had a chance of being selected, who chose to respond, who was selected but did not respond and whether answers were accurate
Match the one clue in the scenario to the one type of bias with that definition

key_conditions.condition: each type of bias has its own defining feature: excluded group, self-selection, nonresponse or inaccurate answers
key_conditions.evidence: the scenario gives exactly one defining clue

misconceptions.description: mixes up units that could not be selected with selected units that did not respond
mixes up self-selection with nonresponse
mixes up inaccurate answers with how units were selected

verification.independent_path: each scenario is built from one defining clue of a four-row table of bias types, and exactly one type matches that clue

ap_statistics-m05.stem: A principal plans an experiment to compare the new study guide with the old study guide on the score on a final exam, using $20$ students in each of two classes taught by different teachers. The score on a final exam is expected to differ between the two classs even without any treatment. Which of the following designs is the best way to carry out the experiment?

options.text: Let the students in each class be assigned to the treatment that the principal expects to work better
options.why: The assignment is not random, so the choice of the experimenter can be confounded with the response.

options.text: Number all of the students in both classs together and randomly assign half of all of them to the new study guide and the rest to the old study guide, ignoring the class
options.why: The assignment is random, but it does not guarantee that each class receives both treatments in equal numbers, so it does not control for the difference between the classs.

options.text: Use the new study guide for all of the students in one class and the old study guide for all of the students in the other class
options.why: Each treatment is used in only one class, so the treatment is confounded with the difference between the classs.

options.text: Within each class, randomly assign half of the students to the new study guide and the other half to the old study guide
options.why: Random assignment within each class gives both treatments the same share of each class, so differences between the classs cannot be mistaken for a treatment effect.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Justify a randomized block design when the response is expected to differ between known groups
student_thinking: Notice that the response is expected to differ between the blocks, so the treatments must be balanced within each block
Check that the assignment is random and that every block receives both treatments

key_conditions.condition: a randomized block design randomly assigns the treatments within each block so that block differences are not confounded with the treatment
key_conditions.evidence: the stem says the response is expected to differ between the blocks

misconceptions.description: uses a different treatment in each block
lets the experimenter choose the treatments
randomizes without regard to the blocks

verification.independent_path: each design is generated from a property table (random assignment, both treatments in every block, block effect separated) and exactly one design has every property

ap_statistics-m06.stem: A seed company states that each of its seeds germinates with probability $0.3$, independently of other seeds. A researcher wants to use a table of random digits, in which each digit from $0$ to $9$ is equally likely, to estimate the probability that at least $2$ of $4$ seeds germinate. Which of the following describes a correct simulation?

options.text: The digits $0$ through $2$ represent that a seed germinates and $3$ through $9$ that it is not; each trial reads $6$ random digits and records whether at least $2$ of them are in the first group, repeated for many trials
options.why: A trial uses a different number of digits than the $4$ seeds in the scenario, so the simulated event is not the one asked about.

options.text: The digits $0$ through $2$ represent that a seed germinates and $3$ through $9$ that it is not; each trial reads $4$ random digits and records whether at least $2$ of them are in the first group, repeated for many trials
options.why: The probability that a seed germinates is $0.3$, so $3$ of the $10$ equally likely digits represent it; one trial has $4$ seeds, and the event counted is at least $2$.

options.text: The digits $0$ through $2$ represent that a seed germinates and $3$ through $9$ that it is not; each trial reads $4$ random digits and records whether exactly $2$ of them are in the first group, repeated for many trials
options.why: Counts a different event: the scenario asks for at least $2$, not exactly $2$.

options.text: The digits $0$ through $4$ represent that a seed germinates and $5$ through $9$ that it is not; each trial reads $4$ random digits and records whether at least $2$ of them are in the first group, repeated for many trials
options.why: The share of digits assigned to the event does not match the stated probability, so the simulation estimates a different probability.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Identify a correct simulation design (digit assignment, trial length and event counted) for a probability question
student_thinking: Assign digits so that the share of digits for the event equals the given probability
Make one trial a set of digits equal to the number of individuals and count the event exactly as the question states

key_conditions.condition: a simulation must reproduce the probability of one outcome, the number of independent repetitions in a trial and the event that is counted
key_conditions.evidence: the stem gives the probability, the number of individuals in a trial and the event

misconceptions.description: assigns the wrong share of digits to the event
uses the wrong number of digits per trial
counts a different event than the one asked about

verification.independent_path: each design is a triple (digits for the event, digits per trial, counting rule) and is accepted as correct only when all three equal the target triple; the three wrong designs each differ in exactly one component

ap_statistics-m07.stem: A teacher wants to know whether a review session changes test scores. Each student's score is recorded on a test before the session and on a similar test after the session, and the difference is found as before minus after. The teacher suspects that the review session raises the mean score. Let $\mu_d$ be the mean difference (before minus after), in points, for all students. Which of the following pairs of hypotheses should be tested?

options.text: $H_0: \bar{x}_d = 0$ and $H_a: \bar{x}_d < 0$
options.why: Writes the hypotheses about a sample mean, but hypotheses are always about the population parameter.

options.text: $H_0: \mu_d = 0$ and $H_a: \mu_d \ne 0$
options.why: Writes a two-sided alternative although the suspicion has a direction.

options.text: $H_0: \mu_d = 0$ and $H_a: \mu_d > 0$
options.why: Reverses the direction of the alternative hypothesis relative to the suspicion. The direction of a mean difference follows the order of subtraction in its definition.

options.text: $H_0: \mu_d = 0$ and $H_a: \mu_d < 0$
options.why: The parameter is the mean difference (before minus after), in points, for all students; the null hypothesis states the claimed value and the alternative matches the suspicion and the order of subtraction in the definition.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Choose the null and alternative hypotheses about a population mean or mean difference
student_thinking: Identify the population parameter (a mean or a mean difference) and the claimed value for the null hypothesis
Use the direction of the suspicion and, for a difference, the order of subtraction to choose the alternative

key_conditions.condition: the null hypothesis states equality with the claimed value and the alternative reflects the suspicion in the direction fixed by how the parameter is defined
key_conditions.evidence: the stem defines the parameter and states the suspicion

misconceptions.description: uses the alternative in the wrong direction
writes hypotheses about a sample mean
uses a two-sided alternative for a directional suspicion

verification.independent_path: each option is generated from a table of direction, symbol and roles; the direction of a paired alternative is derived from the stated order of subtraction and the suspicion

ap_statistics-m08.stem: A $95\%$ confidence interval for the mean number of hours of sleep that students at a university get each night is constructed from a random sample of $49$ students using a one-sample $t$-interval. A researcher then constructs a $90\%$ confidence interval from a new random sample of $16$ students. Assume that the sample standard deviation is the same for both samples and that the conditions for inference are met. Which of the following statements about the width of the new interval compared with the original interval is correct?

options.text: The new interval will have the same width as the original interval
options.why: Assumes the two effects cancel exactly, but the new margin of error is about $1.53$ times the original margin of error.

options.text: The new interval will be narrower than the original interval
options.why: Lets the lower confidence level dominate, but the new margin of error is about $1.53$ times the original margin of error, so the smaller sample size has the larger effect and the interval is wider.

options.text: The new interval will be wider than the original interval
options.why: The smaller sample size has the larger effect: the new margin of error is about $1.53$ times the original margin of error, so the interval is wider.

options.text: The relative width of the new interval cannot be determined without knowing the value of the sample standard deviation
options.why: The sample standard deviation is the same in both intervals, so it cancels from the ratio of the margins of error, and the relative width can be determined.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Judge the net effect on the width of a t-interval when the sample size and the confidence level change together in opposite directions
student_thinking: Recall that a larger sample size reduces the standard error and a higher confidence level increases the critical value
Compare the two margins of error to decide which effect is larger, using the critical values and the square roots of the sample sizes

key_conditions.condition: the margin of error is t-star times s over the square root of n, so the width depends on the critical value and the sample size together
key_conditions.evidence: the stem gives both sample sizes and both confidence levels and says the standard deviations are equal

misconceptions.description: believes the two opposite effects cancel exactly
considers only the change in the sample size or only the confidence level
believes the standard deviation is needed although it cancels

verification.independent_path: the ratio of the margins of error is computed from t critical values found with scipy and again by bisection on the numerically integrated t cdf, and the ratio must differ from 1 by at least 15 percent

ap_statistics-m09.stem: A researcher tests $H_0: \mu = 70$ versus $H_a: \mu > 70$, where $\mu$ is the mean score of all students on a reading test, at significance level $\alpha = 0.05$ using a random sample of $50$ students. The researcher wants to reduce the probability of a Type II error without increasing the probability of a Type I error. Which of the following changes should the researcher make?

options.text: Decrease the significance level while keeping the sample size the same
options.why: A smaller significance level makes it harder to reject the null hypothesis, which raises the probability of a Type II error.

options.text: Decrease the sample size while keeping the significance level the same
options.why: A smaller sample size increases the variability of the sampling distribution, which raises the probability of a Type II error.

options.text: Increase the significance level while keeping the sample size the same
options.why: This lowers the probability of a Type II error, but it raises the probability of a Type I error, which the researcher wants to avoid.

options.text: Increase the sample size while keeping the significance level the same
options.why: A larger sample size reduces the variability of the sampling distribution, which increases power and lowers the probability of a Type II error without changing the probability of a Type I error.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Relate sample size and significance level to the probabilities of Type I and Type II errors
student_thinking: Recall how the sample size and the significance level each change the probability of a Type I error and of a Type II error
Choose the one change that lowers the probability of a Type II error and does not raise the probability of a Type I error

key_conditions.condition: a larger sample size raises power without changing the probability of a Type I error, while a larger significance level raises power only by raising the probability of a Type I error
key_conditions.evidence: the stem states the goal as two requirements on the error probabilities

misconceptions.description: raises the significance level and ignores the Type I error
thinks a smaller significance level raises power
thinks a smaller sample size raises power

verification.independent_path: each change is encoded as a pair (change in sample size, change in significance level) and the effects on both error probabilities are evaluated from a rule table; exactly one change meets both requirements

ap_statistics-m10.stem: A coach wants to test whether the mean time for all of her runners to finish a mile is less than $7$ minutes, using the times of a random sample of $25$ runners. Which of the following procedures is appropriate?

options.text: A one-sample z-test for a population proportion
options.why: Needs a count of successes in a category, but each individual contributes a measurement of a quantitative variable.

options.text: A matched-pairs t-test for a mean difference
options.why: Needs two measurements on the same individual or on matched individuals, but each individual is measured only once, so there are no pairs.

options.text: A two-sample t-test for a difference in population means
options.why: Needs two independent samples to compare, but the scenario has only one sample from one population.

options.text: A one-sample t-test for a population mean
options.why: The variables, the number of samples and the way the data were collected in the scenario match this procedure.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Choose the inference procedure for a mean or a mean difference
student_thinking: Decide whether the data are categorical counts or quantitative measurements, and whether the measurements are paired
Count the samples and the variables, then match the one procedure that fits the data collection

key_conditions.condition: the type of variable, the number of samples, pairing and the number of variables determine the procedure
key_conditions.evidence: the scenario states the variables, the sampling and the goal

misconceptions.description: uses two independent samples where there is a pairing or only one sample
uses matched pairs when there are no pairs
uses a proportion procedure for measurements

verification.independent_path: each procedure is tied to a feature table (variable type, number of samples, pairing, number of variables) and exactly one procedure matches the scenario; each wrong option is rejected by a stated feature

ap_statistics-m11.stem: A school wants to test for an association between the favorite subject (math, science, history or art) and the grade level (freshman, sophomore, junior or senior) of students, using one random sample of $240$ students classified by both variables. Which of the following procedures is appropriate?

options.text: A one-sample z-test for a population proportion
options.why: Tests one proportion for a single categorical variable, but each individual here is classified by two categorical variables.

options.text: A two-sample t-test for a difference in population means
options.why: Compares the means of a quantitative variable in two groups, but both variables in the scenario are categorical.

options.text: A two-sample z-test for a difference in population proportions
options.why: Compares exactly two proportions, but a variable in the scenario has more than two categories, so there is no single difference in proportions to test.

options.text: A chi-square test of independence
options.why: The variables, the number of samples and the way the data were collected in the scenario match this procedure.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Choose the chi-square test of independence for two categorical variables
student_thinking: Decide whether the data are categorical counts or quantitative measurements, and whether the measurements are paired
Count the samples and the variables, then match the one procedure that fits the data collection

key_conditions.condition: the type of variable, the number of samples, pairing and the number of variables determine the procedure
key_conditions.evidence: the scenario states the variables, the sampling and the goal

misconceptions.description: uses a two-proportion procedure when a variable has more than two categories
uses a one-proportion procedure for two variables
uses a means procedure for categorical variables

verification.independent_path: each procedure is tied to a feature table (variable type, number of samples, pairing, number of variables) and exactly one procedure matches the scenario; each wrong option is rejected by a stated feature

ap_statistics-m12.stem: In a school district with $1682$ students, a random sample of $120$ students is selected. Of the sampled students, $8$ ride the bus to school. The sample is used to test $H_0: p = 0.25$ versus $H_a: p \ne 0.25$, where $p$ is the proportion of all district students who ride the bus to school. Which of the following statements about the conditions for a one-sample $z$-test for a proportion is correct?

options.text: The large counts condition is not satisfied, because the number of sampled students who ride the bus to school is $8$, which is less than $10$
options.why: Checks the large counts condition with the sample counts, but a test uses the null value: $np_0 = 30$ and $n(1-p_0) = 90$ are both at least $10$.

options.text: The $10\%$ condition is not satisfied, because $n = 120$ is more than $10\%$ of $N = 1682$
options.why: Claims the $10\%$ condition fails, but $n = 120$ is less than $10\%$ of $N = 1682$, which is $168.2$.

options.text: All three conditions are satisfied, because the sample is random, $n = 120$ is less than $10\%$ of $N = 1682$, and $np_0 = 30$ and $n(1-p_0) = 90$ are both at least $10$
options.why: The sample is random, $n = 120$ is less than $10\%$ of $N = 1682$ (that is, $168.2$), and $np_0 = 30$ and $n(1-p_0) = 90$ are both at least $10$.

options.text: The random condition is not satisfied, because only a small part of all district students was included in the sample
options.why: The sample was selected at random, and a small part of the population being sampled does not make a sample non-random.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Verify the conditions for a one-sample z-test for a proportion
student_thinking: Check random selection, then compare n with ten percent of N for independence
Check large counts with the null value p0, not with the sample proportion, then decide which single condition fails or that none does

key_conditions.condition: a z-test for a proportion needs random selection, n at most 10 percent of N, and np0 and n(1-p0) both at least 10
key_conditions.evidence: the stem gives the sampling method, N, n, the number of successes in the sample and the null value

misconceptions.description: checks large counts with the sample counts instead of the null value
claims the 10 percent condition fails when it holds
treats a small sampled fraction as a random-selection problem

verification.independent_path: each condition is evaluated separately in code from N, n, p0 and the sample count, and exactly one of the four verdicts agrees with all three evaluations; the verdict from the sample counts is checked to disagree with the verdict from p0
verification.method: separate evaluation of each condition plus sample-count trap check
